metadata.title: The Einstein--$\Lambda$ flow on product manifolds

extraction_notes.note: The terms MGHD and recollapse are introduced only inside the sentence stating the Closed Universe Recollapse conjecture; since one sentence cannot be two nodes, no separate definition node was made and the later uses of MGHD carry no definition edge.
Claim or definition: the sentence both introduces $H$, $K$, $\Sigma$ and asserts their formulas for the ansatz via a 'straightforward computation'; kept as a claim.

The sentence introducing the Nariai metric also asserts its known instability and its analogy with the critical solution; the whole sentence is one definition node, and the instability itself is Theorem 1.6 (TP5).

Remarks that carry their own derivations (expansion rate in Case 3, Kasner-type blow-up for Nariai perturbations); kept as remarks because the paper labels them so and no other node relies on them as results.

Introduction summaries of Theorems 1.1 and 1.4 (Sections 1.1-1.2) are restatements and get no node; the cited spherically symmetric recollapse results (Burnett-Rendall, Henkel) are only mentioned, not stated.

Case 2 of the proof of Theorem 1.1 is a single 'easy to see' sentence; step rule 6 (immediate sentences never stand alone) overrides treating it as its own case step, so it is appended to the last Case 1 step.

metadata.extraction_comment: Theorem 1.6 (Nariai instability) is marked external since the paper attributes it to Beyer (2009); its proof PP5 is the paper's own elementary proof.

nodes.name: Einstein flow
nodes.statement: By \emph{Einstein flow} we refer to the form of the Einstein equations when a foliation of spacetime is chosen.
nodes.genus: the form of the Einstein equations
differentia: when a foliation of spacetime is chosen

nodes.name: Closed Universe Recollapse conjecture
nodes.statement: If $M$ is three-dimensional and of positive Yamabe type $Y_+$, it is conjectured that its maximal globally hyperbolic development (MGHD) recollapses, i.e.~is future and past geodesically incomplete \cite{BaGaTi86} (\emph{Closed Universe Recollapse conjecture}).
nodes.statement_short: A 3-dimensional closed universe of positive Yamabe type has a MGHD that recollapses (future and past geodesically incomplete) when $\Lambda=0$.
assumptions: $M$ is three-dimensional and of positive Yamabe type $Y_+$
conclusions: its maximal globally hyperbolic development (MGHD) recollapses, i.e.~is future and past geodesically incomplete

nodes.name: Milne model attractor theorem
nodes.statement: In the negative Yamabe class $Y_-$ it is known that in an open neighborhood of initial data corresponding to the Milne model, this solution serves as an attractor of the Einstein flow \cite{AnMo11}.
nodes.statement_short: Near Milne initial data in the negative Yamabe class, the Milne model attracts the Einstein flow.
assumptions: in an open neighborhood of initial data corresponding to the Milne model
conclusions: this solution serves as an attractor of the Einstein flow

nodes.name: Future completeness conjecture for Y_- and Y_0 (Rendall)
nodes.statement: It is conjectured that under additional restrictions the global geometry of the Milne model (future completeness) is prototypical for the behavior of the Einstein flow in the classes $Y_-$ or $Y_0$ (but the spacetime has to be non-flat) in three spatial dimensions, i.e.~that the spacetimes admit CMC foliations where the mean curvature takes values in $(-\infty,0)$ and that this foliation covers the entire spacetime \cite{Re96}.
nodes.statement_short: In 3 spatial dimensions, classes $Y_-$, $Y_0$ (non-flat) should behave like Milne: CMC foliations with $H\in(-\infty,0)$ covering the spacetime.
assumptions: in the classes $Y_-$ or $Y_0$ (but the spacetime has to be non-flat) in three spatial dimensions
conclusions: the spacetimes admit CMC foliations where the mean curvature takes values in $(-\infty,0)$ and that this foliation covers the entire spacetime

nodes.name: Future nonlinear stability of the known Einstein-Lambda models
nodes.statement: All those models are future nonlinear stable \cite{Ri08}.
conclusions: All those models are future nonlinear stable

nodes.name: Product ansatz with Einstein factors
nodes.statement: The explicit models, which we construct are of product form \eq{ \left(\overline M,\mathbf g\right)=\left(I\times M_1\times M_2,-dt^2+a(t)^2 g_1+b(t)^2g_2\right), } where $g_1$ and $g_2$ are Einstein metrics, i.e.~$\mathrm {Ric}[g_i]=\lambda_i g_i$ for $i=1,2$ and constants $\lambda_i$.

nodes.name: Recollapse and completeness for Einstein-Lambda product models
nodes.statement: Let $\Lambda=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ and let $M_1$, $M_2$ be closed manifolds of dimension $\dim M_i=n_i\geq 2$, $n_1+n_2=n$. Consider initial data of the form $x(0)=y(0)=\dot x(0)=\dot y(0)=0$ such that \eq{ n(n-1)=n_1\lambda_1+n_2\lambda_2, } holds. Then the following cases occur. \begin{enumerate} \item If $\lambda_2>n$ and $\lambda_1<(n_1-1)n/n_1$, the MGHD recollapses, i.e.~is future- and past incomplete, $I=(t_-,t_+)$ for $t_-<0<t_+$. Both singularities are of Kasner-type, i.e.~one factor collapses and the other factor has unbounded volume as $t\rightarrow t_{\pm}$. The mean curvature $H\rightarrow \pm\infty$ as $t\rightarrow t_{\pm}$. The Kretschmann scalar is unbounded towards both singularities. In particular, the MGHDs are $C^2$-inextendible. \item If $\lambda_2=n$ and $\lambda_1=(n_1-1)n/n_1$, MGHD is \eq{ \left(\mathbb R\times M_1\times M_2,-dt^2+\cosh\left(\sqrt{\frac{n}{n_1}}t\right)^2\cdot g_1 + g_2\right), } and in particular future and past complete. \item If $n(n_1-1)/n_1<\lambda_1<(n-1)$ or equivalently $n-1<\lambda_2<n$ the MGHD is future- and past complete. In both time directions, both factors expand exponentially with asymptotic growth rates depending only on the dimensions $n_1$ and $n_2$. \end{enumerate} Furthermore, the behavior is stable in the following sense. Initial data induced by any recollapsing solution in the class above has an open\footnote{Here, open is meant in the sense of $(g,K)\in H^\ell\times H^{\ell-1}$ spaces with $\ell=\ell(n)$ sufficiently large, where $(g,K)$ denote the spatial metric and second fundamental form, respectively.} neighborhood in the initial-data manifold, such that the MGHD of each element in this neighborhood recollapses. Similarly, initial data induced by any complete solution (except the critical solution) has an open neighborhood with elements that give rise to complete MGHDs. The critical solution \eqref{crit-sol} is unstable.
nodes.statement_short: For $\Lambda=n(n-1)/2$, $n_i\ge2$ and static initial data with $n(n-1)=n_1\lambda_1+n_2\lambda_2$: curvature disequilibrium gives recollapse with Kasner singularities, the critical case is the cosh solution, near-equilibrium gives two-sided completeness; recollapse and completeness are stable, the critical solution is unstable.

nodes.label: thm-1

nodes.name: Background solution and the case lambda_2<lambda_1
nodes.statement: The case $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=n-1$ corresponds to the background solution \eq{ -dt^2+ \cosh(t)^2 \cdot (g_1+g_2). } If $\lambda_2<\lambda_1$ we divide into three subcases that relate to the previous cases by interchanging $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ (and $n_1$ and $n_2$) in the statements of the theorem.

nodes.name: Recollapse as curvature disequilibrium
nodes.statement: Relation \eqref{eq-def-rel} provides a simple interpretation for the case $\lambda_1,\lambda_2>0$. Then the first condition in the theorem concerns initial data for which the curvatures of both factors differ substantially while the last condition corresponds to initial data where both factors are of equal or almost equal Ricci-curvature. We conclude that for the case of positive curvature recollapse corresponds to a disequilibrium in curvature between the factors.

nodes.name: Products of non-positive factors are one-sided complete
nodes.statement: Every spacetime of the form \eqref{ansatz} with $\lambda_1,\lambda_2\leq 0$ is complete in one time direction and incomplete in the other.
assumptions: Every spacetime of the form \eqref{ansatz} with $\lambda_1,\lambda_2\leq 0$
conclusions: is complete in one time direction and incomplete in the other.
nodes.label: thm-2

nodes.name: Positive curvature is necessary for recollapse
nodes.statement: The previous theorem implies that within the class given by \eqref{ansatz} positive curvature of at least one factor is a necessary criterion for recollapse.

nodes.name: Nariai solution
nodes.statement: The Nariai solution \eq{ -dt^2+\frac{1}{3}g_{\mathbb S^2}+\cosh^2(\sqrt{3}t)dx^2, } where $g_{\mathbb S^2}$ denotes the metric of constant curvature $1$, is known to be unstable \cite{Be09-1,Be09-2} and shares similar features with the critical solution in Theorem \ref{thm-1}, which has one constant factor and one expanding factor (as Nariai does).
nodes.statement_short: The Nariai metric $-dt^2+\frac13 g_{S^2}+\cosh^2(\sqrt3 t)dx^2$, known to be unstable and analogous to the critical solution of Theorem 1.1.

nodes.name: Instability of the Nariai solution
nodes.statement: The Nariai solution is unstable in the class of product manifolds of the type \eqref{ansatz} on $\mathbb S^1\times \mathbb S^2$, i.e.~there are arbitrarily small perturbations with an incomplete MGHD.
assumptions: in the class of product manifolds of the type \eqref{ansatz} on $\mathbb S^1\times \mathbb S^2$
conclusions: there are arbitrarily small perturbations with an incomplete MGHD.
nodes.label: thm-3

nodes.name: Complete analysis of the 3-dimensional space of product initial data
nodes.statement: A complete analysis of the 3-dimensional space of initial data with this product structure with techniques similar to those used in \cite{AnHe07} is clearly desirable.

nodes.name: Einstein-Lambda equations for the product ansatz
nodes.statement: We set $\Lambda=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ and consider solutions of the form \eqref{ansatz}. Then, recall $x=\log(a)$ and $y=\log(b)$, the Einsteins equations imply the following system of ODEs: \eq{\alg{ x''&=n-\lambda_1e^{-2x}-n_1(x')^2-n_2x'y'\\ y''&=n-\lambda_2e^{-2y}- n_2(y')^2-n_1x'y' }} and the Hamiltonian constraint reduces to \eq{n(n-1)=n_1\lambda_1e^{-2x}+n_2\lambda_2e^{-2y}+(n_1-1)n_1(x')^2+(n_2-1)n_2(y')^2+2n_1n_2x'y',} where $x'$ denotes the time derivative of $x$.
nodes.statement_short: For the product ansatz the Einstein-$\Lambda$ equations reduce to a second-order ODE system for $x,y$ plus a Hamiltonian constraint.

nodes.statement: The equations are a direct consequence of \cite[Proposition 2.5]{DoUe05} using the ansatz \eqref{ansatz} for the metric.
nodes.statement_short: Direct application of the warped-product curvature formula of Dobarro-Ünal to the ansatz.

nodes.name: Hawking singularity theorem with positive cosmological constant
nodes.statement: Let $(\overline M^{n+1},\mathbf{g})$ be a $n+1$-dimensional globally hyperbolic Lorentzian manifold and suppose \eq{Ric(X,X)\geq -n |\mathbf g(X,X)|} for all timelike vectors $X$. Assume furthermore that there exists a hypersurface $M$ whose expansion satisfies $\theta\leq \theta_0<-n$. Then, $(\overline M,\mathbf g)$ is future geodesically incomplete.
nodes.section: 2.2 The Hawking singularity theorem with positive cosmological constant
assumptions: Let $(\overline M^{n+1},\mathbf{g})$ be a $n+1$-dimensional globally hyperbolic Lorentzian manifold
there exists a hypersurface $M$ whose expansion satisfies $\theta\leq \theta_0<-n$
conclusions: $(\overline M,\mathbf g)$ is future geodesically incomplete.
nodes.label: sing-thm

nodes.name: Negative scalar curvature Cauchy surface implies one-sided incompleteness
nodes.statement: Let $(\overline{M},\mathbf{g})$ be a MGHD of Einstein's equations with cosmological constant $\Lambda=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}>0$. If $\overline{M}$ contains a Cauchy hypersurface $M$ whose induced metric has scalar curvature $R(g)<R_0<0$, then $\overline{M}$ is geodesically incomplete either to the future or to the past.
nodes.section: 2.2 The Hawking singularity theorem with positive cosmological constant
assumptions: Let $(\overline{M},\mathbf{g})$ be a MGHD of Einstein's equations with cosmological constant $\Lambda=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}>0$.
If $\overline{M}$ contains a Cauchy hypersurface $M$ whose induced metric has scalar curvature $R(g)<R_0<0$
conclusions: $\overline{M}$ is geodesically incomplete either to the future or to the past.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 2.2
nodes.statement: Let $g$ be the induced metric on $M$ and as above, let $K$ be the second fundamental form of $M$ and $\Sigma=K-\frac{1}{n}H$ its tracefree part. By the constraint equations, \eq{n(n-1)=R(g)-|K|^2+H^2=R(g)-|\Sigma|^2+\frac{n-1}{n}H^2\leq R_0+ \frac{n-1}{n}H^2,} so that \eq{\theta^2=H^2\geq (n(n-1)-R_0)\frac{n}{n-1}>n^2.} After time reflection, if necessary, we may conclude \eq{\theta\leq \theta_0<-n} and now future incompleteness follows from the above singularity theorem.
nodes.section: 2.2 The Hawking singularity theorem with positive cosmological constant
nodes.statement_short: Constraint equation bounds $H^2>n^2$; after time reflection the expansion is below $-n$ and the singularity theorem applies.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.1
nodes.statement:
oindent We first prove Case 1. By assumptions on the $\lambda_i$, $y''(0)=n-\lambda_2<0$ and $x''(0)=n-\lambda_1> rac{n}{n_1}>0$. Then, $x$ is monotonically increasing: If $t_0>0$ is the first time such that $x'(t_0)=0$, we get $x''(t_0)> rac{n}{n_1}>0$ (if $\lambda_1\leq0$, we even get $x''(t_0)\geq n)$ which implies $x'(t)<0$ for $t\in (t_0-\varepsilon,t_0)$ and thus contradicts the assumption. Analogously, one shows that $y$ is monotonically decreasing. Now we show that as long as $y$ is uniformly bounded, its derivatives exist and $x$ and its derivatives cannot blow up in finite time. If $y'\leq-1$ and $y\geq Y_0$, we obtain by monotonicity, the evolution equation and $x'y'<0$ that \eq{y''\geq -C (y')^2} which after dividing by $y'$ and integration in turn implies \eq{\log|y'|\leq C(1-Y_0),} i.e. $y'$ is bounded. Observe that by the evolution equation, we get $x''\leq n+Cx'$ as long as $y'>-C$ which implies the assertion on $x$. Next we show that $y$ is unbounded. If not, it must converge to a limit by monotonicity, so we have $y(\infty)=\lim_{t	o\infty} y(t)$. Then we get either a sequence of $t_i	o\infty$ such that $y''(t_i)=0$ or $\lim_{t	o\infty} y''(t)=0$. The first case cannot occur, since then $y''(t_i)=n-\lambda_2e^{-2y(t_0)}\geq  rac{n}{n_1}>0$. In the latter case, we necessarily get $\lim x'(t)=\infty$ by the evolution of $y$. On the other hand, by the constraint equation, \eq{n_1x''-n_2y''=n(n_1-n_2)-n_1\lambda_1e^{-2x}+n_2\lambda_2e^{-2y}-n_1^2(x')^2+n_2^2(y')^2\ \leq C-n_1^2(x')^2+n_2^2(y')^2} From the constraint and adding the evolution equations, we also easily obtain \eq{n_1(x''+(x')^2)+n_2(y''+(y')^2)=n,} from which we get \eq{-n_1(x')^2-2n_2y''+n-n_2(y')^2\leq C-n_1^2(x')^2+n_2^2(y')^2} and therefore, since $n_1>1$ (if $n_1=1$, the above bound implies $\lambda_1<0$ which in turn contradicts $n_1=1$), we get a bound on $x'$ if $y'$ and $y''$ are bounded. This yields the contradiction. By monotonicity of $x$ and $y$ and the unboundedness of $y$ from below there is a constant $C>0$ and a time $t_1>0$ such that the differential inequality \eq{ n_1x''+n_2y''\leq-C-(n_1x'+n_2y')^2 } holds for all $t\geq t_1$. By ODE comparison, $z(t)=n_1x'(t)+n_2y'(t)\leq -\sqrt{C}	an(D+\sqrt{C}(t-t_1))$ for $t\geq t_1$ and some $D\in\mathbb{R}$. Therefore, $z	o-\infty$ as $t$ approaches some $t_+$. As $x'>0$, $y'	o-\infty$. We also have $y(t)\leq rac{1}{n_2}\int_0^{t}z(s)ds	o-\infty$ as $t	o t_+$, which implies that $y$ diverges. In addition, because \eq{x''=n-\lambda_1e^{-2x}-zx'\geq -zx',} we obtain $x(t)\geq \int_0^t\exp(-\int_0^sz(r)dr)ds	o \infty$ as $t	o t_+$. It remains to show that the Kretschmann scalar is unbounded at the singularity: Let $0$ be the index referring to the $t$-coordinate and $i,j$ and $a,b$ be indices referring to coordinates on $M_1,M_2$ respectively. One can check that the coefficients with an odd number of zeros vanish and therefore, the Kretschmann scalar satisfies \eq{ |	ilde{R}|^2=	ilde{R}_{\mu
u\lambda\sigma}	ilde{R}^{\mu
u\lambda\sigma}\geq 0} because all summands are nonnegative. Now it can be checked that \eq{ 	ilde{R}_{0ij0}=- rac{\partial^2_t a}{a} 	ilde{g}_{ij},\qquad 	ilde{R}_{0ab0}=- rac{\partial^2_t b}{b} 	ilde{g}_{ab},} so that \eq{|	ilde{R}|^2\geq \left(n_1 rac{\partial^2_t a}{a}ight)^2+n_2\left( rac{\partial^2_t b}{b}ight)^2=n_1(x''+(x')^2)^2+n_2(y''+(y')^2)^2} where as above $x=\log(a)$, $y=\log(b)$. Now, since $x	o\infty$ as $t	o t_+$, we also get $x''+(x')^2	o\infty$, which shows that the Kretschmann scalar must blow up. This finishes the proof in Case 1. In Case 2, it is easy to see that the metric given in the statement of the theorem is the MGHD of the given initial data. Let us now consider Case 3. By assumption, \eq{ y''(0)=n-\lambda_2\in(0,1) } and \eq{ x''(0)=n-\lambda_1\in (1, rac{n}{n_1}). } Both $x$ and $y$ are strictly monotonically increasing. We have $x'(t)>0$ for small $t$. Let $t_0$ be the first time, where $x'(t_0)=0$. Then we obtain \eq{ x''(t_0)=n-\lambda_1e^{-2x(t_0)}>0, } as long as $y'(t_0)$ exists. Thus $x'<0$ on $(t_0-\varepsilon,t_0)$, which causes the contradiction. Analogously one shows that $y$ is strictly monotonically increasing. From the evolution equations and monotonicity we deduce \eq{ n^2-n_1\lambda_1-n_2\lambda_2-(n_1x'+n_2y')^2\leq n_1x''+n_2y''\leq n^2-(n_1x'+n_2y')^2. } The solution of the corresponding ODE, $z'=n^2-z^2$, is $z(t)=n	anh(nt+c)$, where $c\in \mathbb{R}$. By the initial conditions this implies $0<n_1x'+n_2y'<n$ for all $t>0$. Due to the positivity of $x'$ and $y'$ these statements hold for $x'$ and $y'$ individually. In particular, $x$ and $y$ exist for all times, which finishes the proof of Case 3. Finally, recollapse of MGHDs of small perturbations of the initial data induced by the models follows by the Cauchy stability of the Einstein equations in combination with Theorem ef{sing-thm}. As the background solutions have Cauchy surfaces of strictly positive and strictly negative mean curvature, this also holds for the MGHDs of small perturbations. Then the singularity theorem yields incompleteness. This idea of proof is explained in further detail originally in \cite{Ri09}. Stability in the expanding direction follows from the results in \cite{Ri08}.
nodes.statement_short: Case-by-case ODE analysis of the evolution and constraint equations: monotonicity, ODE comparison to blow-up (Case 1) or tanh bounds (Case 3). Stability follows from Cauchy stability plus the singularity theorem; the key step is the Riccati-type comparison for $z=n_1x'+n_2y'$.

nodes.name: Exponential expansion rate in Case 3
nodes.statement: With some more effort, we can determine the expansion rate of the warping factors of the solutions appearing in Case 3: By the above, we have $n_1x'(t)+n_2y'(t)>C_1>0$ for all $t\geq t_1$ and $n_1x(t)+n_2y(t)>C_2t$ for all $t\geq t_1$ and $C_2>0$. Using this, we can improve the above estimate. Denoting $z=n_1x'+n_2y'$ as above, we get \eq{ n^2-Ce^{-Ct}-z^2\leq z'\leq n^2-z^2. } from which we obtain the uniform bounds $0\geq z-n\geq -Ce^{-Ct}$. After integrating, \eq{0\geq n_1x+n_2y-nt\geq -C.} Similarly, we obtain for $w:=n_1x'-n_2y'$ the estimate \eq{ n(n_1-n_2)-Ce^{-C t} -zw \leq w'\leq n(n_1-n_2)+Ce^{-C t} -zw} which implies because of the estimate on $n-z$ that $|w-(n_1-n_2)|\leq Ce^{-Ct}$. Again by integrating, \eq{{C_1\geq n_1x-n_2y-(n_1-n_2)t\geq C_2.}} Finally, we obtain from \eqref{z} and \eqref{w} that $\sup \left\{|x-t|,|y-t|\right\}\leq C$. It is immediate that the warping functions satisfy $C_1 e^t\leq a(t) \leq C_2e^t$ and $C_1 e^t\leq b(t) \leq C_2e^t$ for $t\geq0$.
nodes.statement_short: In Case 3 both warping functions grow like $e^t$: $C_1e^t\le a,b\le C_2e^t$.
nodes.label: expansionrate

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.4
nodes.statement: If $\lambda_1,\lambda_2\leq 0$, we are going to show that all corresponding solutions are geodesically incomplete in one direction and geodesically complete in the other. Let us first remark that the case where $R(g)\equiv |\Sigma|\equiv 0$ corresponds to the solution $-dt^2+e^{2t}g$ which is geodesically incomplete in the past and geodesically complete in the future. Therefore we assume $R(g)-|\Sigma|^2\leq R_0<0$ from now on. By the constraint equation, we have \eq{n(n-1)=R(g)-|K|^2+H^2=R(g)-|\Sigma|^2+\frac{n-1}{n}H^2\leq R_0+ \frac{n-1}{n}H^2,} As above, we get $|\theta|\geq \theta_0>n$. If $\theta\leq-\theta_0<-n$, we obtain geodesic incompleteness by Proposition \ref{sing-thm}. If $\theta\geq\theta_0>n$, we have the differential inequality \eq{ \partial_t \theta\leq n-\frac{1}{n}\theta^2} so that we have the upper bound \eq{\theta \leq n\cdot\frac{e^{2t}-A_0}{e^{2t}+A_0}= \frac{n}{1-|A_0|e^{-2t}}(1+|A_0|e^{-2t})\leq n+n|A_0|e^{-2t}} where $A_0=\frac{n-\theta_0}{n+\theta_0}$. Again by the constraint equation, \eq{0\leq-R(g)+|\Sigma|^2= \frac{n-1}{n}(\theta^2-n^2)\leq Ce^{-2t}. } In particular, since $R(g)=n_1\lambda_1e^{-2x}+n_2\lambda_2 e^{-2y}$, both factors $x,y$ grow linearly, in particular, they do not converge to $-\infty$. Thus, they are geodesically complete.
nodes.statement_short: Constraint gives $|\theta|>n$; negative expansion gives incompleteness via the singularity theorem, positive expansion is shown complete by a Riccati bound on $\theta$.

nodes.name: Exponential convergence for non-positive factors
nodes.statement: Since $\theta\to n$ and $ |\Sigma|^2\to 0$ exponentially, one concludes that $x',y'\to 1$ exponentially and $\sup \left\{|x-t|,|y-t|\right\}\leq C$ as in Remark \ref{expansionrate}.

nodes.name: Expected Kasner-type singularity
nodes.statement: We expect that the generic type of singularity that occurs in the geodesically incomplete direction is of Kasner type, i.e. one of the factors goes to $\infty$ while the other goes to $-\infty$ as $t\to t_+$. This also implies a blow-up of the Kretschmann scalar as in the proof of Theorem \ref{thm-1}.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.6
nodes.statement: We have the data $n_1=2$, $n_2=1$, $\lambda_1=\lambda$, $\lambda_2=0$, so the evolution equations are \eq{\alg{x''&=3-\lambda e^{-2x}-2(x')^2-x'y'\\ y''&=3-(y')^2-2x'y'}} and the constraint equation reduce to \eq{6=2\lambda e^{-2x}+2(x')^2+4x'y'.} We demand $y'(0)=0$ such that we obtain a one-parameter family of solutions by prescribing $\lambda$ and $x'(0)$ such that \eq{3=\lambda+(x'(0))^2} by the constraint. Recall that we generally require $x(0)=0$. For our purposes, we additionally assume $\lambda>0$ throughout. By using the constraint, the equation on $x$ decouples as \eq{\alg{x''&=3-\lambda e^{-2x}-2(x')^2-x'y'=\frac{1}{2}(3-\lambda e^{-2x}-3(x')^2).}} Now we show that the MGHD is future incomplete, if $\lambda<3$ and $x'(0)<0$. At first, \eq{x''(0)=3-\lambda-2x'(0)^2=(3-\lambda-(x'(0))^2)-x'(0)^2<0,} which shows that both $x$ and $x'$ are monotonically decreasing for small time. In addition, as long as $x$ and $x'$ are monotonically decreasing, we have \eq{x''=\frac{1}{2}(3-\lambda e^{-2x}-3(x')^2)\leq\frac{1}{2}(3-\lambda-2(x'(0)))\leq \frac{1}{2}x''(0)<0,} which shows that this monotonicity property holds for all time and $x$ and $x'$ are unbounded. In particular, for large time, we get \eq{x''\leq -\frac{3}{2}(x')^2. } This shows that $x'\to -\infty$ as $t$ approaches some $t_+$, since the comparison ODE is solved by $z(t)=\frac{2}{c+3t}$. By integrating, one obtains the estimate \eq{x(t)\leq C_1+\log(C_2-\frac{3}{2}t)} for some constants $C_1,C_2>0$ which shows that also $x\to-\infty$ as $t\to t_+$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to a one-parameter family with $y'(0)=0$, decouple the $x$-equation via the constraint, and show $x,x'\to-\infty$ in finite time by monotonicity and ODE comparison.

nodes.name: Kasner type of the Nariai perturbation singularity
nodes.statement: We are also able to show that this singularity is of Kasner type, i.e. $y(t)\to\infty$ as $t\to t_+$. At first note that $y$ is monotonically increasing for small time. In fact, it is monotonically increasing for all $t>0$ since $y''(t_0)=3>0$ as long as $y'(t_0)=0$. But then we have an estimate \eq{y'' \geq 3-(y')^2+2 |z|y'} and since $z\to\infty$ as $t\to t_+$ this shows that $y'\to\infty$ as $t\to t_+$ and because the integral of $z$ diverges, we get that also $y$ diverges as $t\to t_+$.

nodes.name: Past completeness and growth for the Nariai perturbations
nodes.statement: A similar analysis as in the proof of Theorem \ref{thm-1} shows that every MGHD is complete in the other time-direction and arguments as in Remark \ref{expansionrate} imply exponential growth of both warping functions in the past.

nodes.name: Cases 1 and 2
nodes.statement: We first prove Case 1. By assumptions on the $\lambda_i$, $y''(0)=n-\lambda_2<0$ and $x''(0)=n-\lambda_1>\frac{n}{n_1}>0$. Then, $x$ is monotonically increasing: If $t_0>0$ is the first time such that $x'(t_0)=0$, we get $x''(t_0)>\frac{n}{n_1}>0$ (if $\lambda_1\leq0$, we even get $x''(t_0)\geq n)$ which implies $x'(t)<0$ for $t\in (t_0-\varepsilon,t_0)$ and thus contradicts the assumption. Analogously, one shows that $y$ is monotonically decreasing. Now we show that as long as $y$ is uniformly bounded, its derivatives exist and $x$ and its derivatives cannot blow up in finite time. If $y'\leq-1$ and $y\geq Y_0$, we obtain by monotonicity, the evolution equation and $x'y'<0$ that \eq{y''\geq -C (y')^2} which after dividing by $y'$ and integration in turn implies \eq{\log|y'|\leq C(1-Y_0),} i.e. $y'$ is bounded. Observe that by the evolution equation, we get $x''\leq n+Cx'$ as long as $y'>-C$ which implies the assertion on $x$. Next we show that $y$ is unbounded. If not, it must converge to a limit by monotonicity, so we have $y(\infty)=\lim_{t\to\infty} y(t)$. Then we get either a sequence of $t_i\to\infty$ such that $y''(t_i)=0$ or $\lim_{t\to\infty} y''(t)=0$. The first case cannot occur, since then $y''(t_i)=n-\lambda_2e^{-2y(t_0)}\geq \frac{n}{n_1}>0$. In the latter case, we necessarily get $\lim x'(t)=\infty$ by the evolution of $y$. On the other hand, by the constraint equation, \eq{n_1x''-n_2y''=n(n_1-n_2)-n_1\lambda_1e^{-2x}+n_2\lambda_2e^{-2y}-n_1^2(x')^2+n_2^2(y')^2\\ \leq C-n_1^2(x')^2+n_2^2(y')^2} From the constraint and adding the evolution equations, we also easily obtain \eq{n_1(x''+(x')^2)+n_2(y''+(y')^2)=n,} from which we get \eq{-n_1(x')^2-2n_2y''+n-n_2(y')^2\leq C-n_1^2(x')^2+n_2^2(y')^2} and therefore, since $n_1>1$ (if $n_1=1$, the above bound implies $\lambda_1<0$ which in turn contradicts $n_1=1$), we get a bound on $x'$ if $y'$ and $y''$ are bounded. This yields the contradiction. By monotonicity of $x$ and $y$ and the unboundedness of $y$ from below there is a constant $C>0$ and a time $t_1>0$ such that the differential inequality \eq{ n_1x''+n_2y''\leq-C-(n_1x'+n_2y')^2 } holds for all $t\geq t_1$. By ODE comparison, $z(t)=n_1x'(t)+n_2y'(t)\leq -\sqrt{C}\tan(D+\sqrt{C}(t-t_1))$ for $t\geq t_1$ and some $D\in\mathbb{R}$. Therefore, $z\to-\infty$ as $t$ approaches some $t_+$. As $x'>0$, $y'\to-\infty$. We also have $y(t)\leq\frac{1}{n_2}\int_0^{t}z(s)ds\to-\infty$ as $t\to t_+$, which implies that $y$ diverges. In addition, because \eq{x''=n-\lambda_1e^{-2x}-zx'\geq -zx',} we obtain $x(t)\geq \int_0^t\exp(-\int_0^sz(r)dr)ds\to \infty$ as $t\to t_+$. It remains to show that the Kretschmann scalar is unbounded at the singularity: Let $0$ be the index referring to the $t$-coordinate and $i,j$ and $a,b$ be indices referring to coordinates on $M_1,M_2$ respectively. One can check that the coefficients with an odd number of zeros vanish and therefore, the Kretschmann scalar satisfies \eq{ |\tilde{R}|^2=\tilde{R}_{\mu\nu\lambda\sigma}\tilde{R}^{\mu\nu\lambda\sigma}\geq 0} because all summands are nonnegative. Now it can be checked that \eq{ \tilde{R}_{0ij0}=-\frac{\partial^2_t a}{a} \tilde{g}_{ij},\qquad \tilde{R}_{0ab0}=-\frac{\partial^2_t b}{b} \tilde{g}_{ab},} so that \eq{|\tilde{R}|^2\geq \left(n_1\frac{\partial^2_t a}{a}\right)^2+n_2\left(\frac{\partial^2_t b}{b}\right)^2=n_1(x''+(x')^2)^2+n_2(y''+(y')^2)^2} where as above $x=\log(a)$, $y=\log(b)$. Now, since $x\to\infty$ as $t\to t_+$, we also get $x''+(x')^2\to\infty$, which shows that the Kretschmann scalar must blow up. This finishes the proof in Case 1. In Case 2, it is easy to see that the metric given in the statement of the theorem is the MGHD of the given initial data.
nodes.statement_short: Case 1: recollapse with Kasner-type singularities; Case 2 is immediate.

nodes.name: Monotonicity of x and y
nodes.statement: We first prove Case 1. By assumptions on the $\lambda_i$, $y''(0)=n-\lambda_2<0$ and $x''(0)=n-\lambda_1>\frac{n}{n_1}>0$. Then, $x$ is monotonically increasing: If $t_0>0$ is the first time such that $x'(t_0)=0$, we get $x''(t_0)>\frac{n}{n_1}>0$ (if $\lambda_1\leq0$, we even get $x''(t_0)\geq n)$ which implies $x'(t)<0$ for $t\in (t_0-\varepsilon,t_0)$ and thus contradicts the assumption. Analogously, one shows that $y$ is monotonically decreasing.
nodes.statement_short: $x$ increases and $y$ decreases.

nodes.name: No blow-up while y bounded
nodes.statement: Now we show that as long as $y$ is uniformly bounded, its derivatives exist and $x$ and its derivatives cannot blow up in finite time. If $y'\leq-1$ and $y\geq Y_0$, we obtain by monotonicity, the evolution equation and $x'y'<0$ that \eq{y''\geq -C (y')^2} which after dividing by $y'$ and integration in turn implies \eq{\log|y'|\leq C(1-Y_0),} i.e. $y'$ is bounded. Observe that by the evolution equation, we get $x''\leq n+Cx'$ as long as $y'>-C$ which implies the assertion on $x$.
nodes.statement_short: Show $x$ and derivatives cannot blow up while $y$ is bounded.

nodes.name: Bound on y'
nodes.statement: If $y'\leq-1$ and $y\geq Y_0$, we obtain by monotonicity, the evolution equation and $x'y'<0$ that \eq{y''\geq -C (y')^2} which after dividing by $y'$ and integration in turn implies \eq{\log|y'|\leq C(1-Y_0),} i.e. $y'$ is bounded.
nodes.statement_short: Integrate $y''\ge -C(y')^2$ to bound $y'$.

nodes.name: Bound on x
nodes.statement: Observe that by the evolution equation, we get $x''\leq n+Cx'$ as long as $y'>-C$ which implies the assertion on $x$.
nodes.statement_short: Linear growth bound on $x'$.

nodes.name: y is unbounded
nodes.statement: Next we show that $y$ is unbounded. If not, it must converge to a limit by monotonicity, so we have $y(\infty)=\lim_{t\to\infty} y(t)$. Then we get either a sequence of $t_i\to\infty$ such that $y''(t_i)=0$ or $\lim_{t\to\infty} y''(t)=0$. The first case cannot occur, since then $y''(t_i)=n-\lambda_2e^{-2y(t_0)}\geq \frac{n}{n_1}>0$. In the latter case, we necessarily get $\lim x'(t)=\infty$ by the evolution of $y$. On the other hand, by the constraint equation, \eq{n_1x''-n_2y''=n(n_1-n_2)-n_1\lambda_1e^{-2x}+n_2\lambda_2e^{-2y}-n_1^2(x')^2+n_2^2(y')^2\\ \leq C-n_1^2(x')^2+n_2^2(y')^2} From the constraint and adding the evolution equations, we also easily obtain \eq{n_1(x''+(x')^2)+n_2(y''+(y')^2)=n,} from which we get \eq{-n_1(x')^2-2n_2y''+n-n_2(y')^2\leq C-n_1^2(x')^2+n_2^2(y')^2} and therefore, since $n_1>1$ (if $n_1=1$, the above bound implies $\lambda_1<0$ which in turn contradicts $n_1=1$), we get a bound on $x'$ if $y'$ and $y''$ are bounded. This yields the contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Show $y$ is unbounded by contradiction.

nodes.name: Assume y converges
nodes.statement: If not, it must converge to a limit by monotonicity, so we have $y(\infty)=\lim_{t\to\infty} y(t)$. Then we get either a sequence of $t_i\to\infty$ such that $y''(t_i)=0$ or $\lim_{t\to\infty} y''(t)=0$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume $y$ converges; then $y''$ vanishes along a sequence or in the limit.

nodes.name: Exclude both cases
nodes.statement: The first case cannot occur, since then $y''(t_i)=n-\lambda_2e^{-2y(t_0)}\geq \frac{n}{n_1}>0$. In the latter case, we necessarily get $\lim x'(t)=\infty$ by the evolution of $y$.
nodes.statement_short: First alternative impossible; second forces $x'\to\infty$.

nodes.name: Constraint bounds x'
nodes.statement: On the other hand, by the constraint equation, \eq{n_1x''-n_2y''=n(n_1-n_2)-n_1\lambda_1e^{-2x}+n_2\lambda_2e^{-2y}-n_1^2(x')^2+n_2^2(y')^2\\ \leq C-n_1^2(x')^2+n_2^2(y')^2} From the constraint and adding the evolution equations, we also easily obtain \eq{n_1(x''+(x')^2)+n_2(y''+(y')^2)=n,} from which we get \eq{-n_1(x')^2-2n_2y''+n-n_2(y')^2\leq C-n_1^2(x')^2+n_2^2(y')^2} and therefore, since $n_1>1$ (if $n_1=1$, the above bound implies $\lambda_1<0$ which in turn contradicts $n_1=1$), we get a bound on $x'$ if $y'$ and $y''$ are bounded. This yields the contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Constraint and evolution equations bound $x'$, contradiction.

nodes.name: Finite-time blow-up by ODE comparison
nodes.statement: By monotonicity of $x$ and $y$ and the unboundedness of $y$ from below there is a constant $C>0$ and a time $t_1>0$ such that the differential inequality \eq{ n_1x''+n_2y''\leq-C-(n_1x'+n_2y')^2 } holds for all $t\geq t_1$. By ODE comparison, $z(t)=n_1x'(t)+n_2y'(t)\leq -\sqrt{C}\tan(D+\sqrt{C}(t-t_1))$ for $t\geq t_1$ and some $D\in\mathbb{R}$. Therefore, $z\to-\infty$ as $t$ approaches some $t_+$. As $x'>0$, $y'\to-\infty$. We also have $y(t)\leq\frac{1}{n_2}\int_0^{t}z(s)ds\to-\infty$ as $t\to t_+$, which implies that $y$ diverges.
nodes.statement_short: Riccati comparison for $z=n_1x'+n_2y'$ gives blow-up at $t_+$; $y\to-\infty$.

nodes.name: x diverges
nodes.statement: In addition, because \eq{x''=n-\lambda_1e^{-2x}-zx'\geq -zx',} we obtain $x(t)\geq \int_0^t\exp(-\int_0^sz(r)dr)ds\to \infty$ as $t\to t_+$.
nodes.statement_short: $x\to\infty$ as $t\to t_+$.

nodes.name: Reduce to Kretschmann blow-up
nodes.statement: It remains to show that the Kretschmann scalar is unbounded at the singularity:
nodes.statement_short: Remains to show Kretschmann scalar blow-up.

nodes.name: Kretschmann scalar is a sum of squares
nodes.statement: Let $0$ be the index referring to the $t$-coordinate and $i,j$ and $a,b$ be indices referring to coordinates on $M_1,M_2$ respectively. One can check that the coefficients with an odd number of zeros vanish and therefore, the Kretschmann scalar satisfies \eq{ |\tilde{R}|^2=\tilde{R}_{\mu\nu\lambda\sigma}\tilde{R}^{\mu\nu\lambda\sigma}\geq 0} because all summands are nonnegative.
nodes.statement_short: Index conventions; Kretschmann scalar is a nonnegative sum.

nodes.name: Lower bound for the Kretschmann scalar
nodes.statement: Now it can be checked that \eq{ \tilde{R}_{0ij0}=-\frac{\partial^2_t a}{a} \tilde{g}_{ij},\qquad \tilde{R}_{0ab0}=-\frac{\partial^2_t b}{b} \tilde{g}_{ab},} so that \eq{|\tilde{R}|^2\geq \left(n_1\frac{\partial^2_t a}{a}\right)^2+n_2\left(\frac{\partial^2_t b}{b}\right)^2=n_1(x''+(x')^2)^2+n_2(y''+(y')^2)^2} where as above $x=\log(a)$, $y=\log(b)$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound $|\tilde R|^2$ below by $x''+(x')^2$ terms.

nodes.name: Kretschmann blow-up; Case 2
nodes.statement: Now, since $x\to\infty$ as $t\to t_+$, we also get $x''+(x')^2\to\infty$, which shows that the Kretschmann scalar must blow up. This finishes the proof in Case 1. In Case 2, it is easy to see that the metric given in the statement of the theorem is the MGHD of the given initial data.
nodes.statement_short: $x\to\infty$ forces Kretschmann blow-up; Case 2's metric is checked directly.

nodes.name: Case 3
nodes.statement: Let us now consider Case 3. By assumption, \eq{ y''(0)=n-\lambda_2\in(0,1) } and \eq{ x''(0)=n-\lambda_1\in (1,\frac{n}{n_1}). } Both $x$ and $y$ are strictly monotonically increasing. We have $x'(t)>0$ for small $t$. Let $t_0$ be the first time, where $x'(t_0)=0$. Then we obtain \eq{ x''(t_0)=n-\lambda_1e^{-2x(t_0)}>0, } as long as $y'(t_0)$ exists. Thus $x'<0$ on $(t_0-\varepsilon,t_0)$, which causes the contradiction. Analogously one shows that $y$ is strictly monotonically increasing. From the evolution equations and monotonicity we deduce \eq{ n^2-n_1\lambda_1-n_2\lambda_2-(n_1x'+n_2y')^2\leq n_1x''+n_2y''\leq n^2-(n_1x'+n_2y')^2. } The solution of the corresponding ODE, $z'=n^2-z^2$, is $z(t)=n\tanh(nt+c)$, where $c\in \mathbb{R}$. By the initial conditions this implies $0<n_1x'+n_2y'<n$ for all $t>0$. Due to the positivity of $x'$ and $y'$ these statements hold for $x'$ and $y'$ individually. In particular, $x$ and $y$ exist for all times, which finishes the proof of Case 3.
nodes.statement_short: Case 3: global existence and expansion in both directions.

nodes.name: Initial accelerations
nodes.statement: Let us now consider Case 3. By assumption, \eq{ y''(0)=n-\lambda_2\in(0,1) } and \eq{ x''(0)=n-\lambda_1\in (1,\frac{n}{n_1}). }

nodes.name: Strict monotonicity
nodes.statement: Both $x$ and $y$ are strictly monotonically increasing. We have $x'(t)>0$ for small $t$. Let $t_0$ be the first time, where $x'(t_0)=0$. Then we obtain \eq{ x''(t_0)=n-\lambda_1e^{-2x(t_0)}>0, } as long as $y'(t_0)$ exists. Thus $x'<0$ on $(t_0-\varepsilon,t_0)$, which causes the contradiction. Analogously one shows that $y$ is strictly monotonically increasing.
nodes.statement_short: First zero of $x'$ leads to contradiction; $x,y$ increase.

nodes.name: tanh comparison and global existence
nodes.statement: From the evolution equations and monotonicity we deduce \eq{ n^2-n_1\lambda_1-n_2\lambda_2-(n_1x'+n_2y')^2\leq n_1x''+n_2y''\leq n^2-(n_1x'+n_2y')^2. } The solution of the corresponding ODE, $z'=n^2-z^2$, is $z(t)=n\tanh(nt+c)$, where $c\in \mathbb{R}$. By the initial conditions this implies $0<n_1x'+n_2y'<n$ for all $t>0$. Due to the positivity of $x'$ and $y'$ these statements hold for $x'$ and $y'$ individually. In particular, $x$ and $y$ exist for all times, which finishes the proof of Case 3.
nodes.statement_short: Comparison with $z'=n^2-z^2$ gives $0<n_1x'+n_2y'<n$, so solutions exist for all time.

nodes.name: Stability via Cauchy stability
nodes.statement: Finally, recollapse of MGHDs of small perturbations of the initial data induced by the models follows by the Cauchy stability of the Einstein equations in combination with Theorem \ref{sing-thm}. As the background solutions have Cauchy surfaces of strictly positive and strictly negative mean curvature, this also holds for the MGHDs of small perturbations. Then the singularity theorem yields incompleteness. This idea of proof is explained in further detail originally in \cite{Ri09}. Stability in the expanding direction follows from the results in \cite{Ri08}.
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy stability plus the singularity theorem give stable recollapse; Ringström gives stable expansion.

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement: If $\lambda_1,\lambda_2\leq 0$, we are going to show that all corresponding solutions are geodesically incomplete in one direction and geodesically complete in the other.
nodes.statement_short: State the goal.

nodes.name: Trivial case and expansion bound
nodes.statement: Let us first remark that the case where $R(g)\equiv |\Sigma|\equiv 0$ corresponds to the solution $-dt^2+e^{2t}g$ which is geodesically incomplete in the past and geodesically complete in the future. Therefore we assume $R(g)-|\Sigma|^2\leq R_0<0$ from now on. By the constraint equation, we have \eq{n(n-1)=R(g)-|K|^2+H^2=R(g)-|\Sigma|^2+\frac{n-1}{n}H^2\leq R_0+ \frac{n-1}{n}H^2,} As above, we get $|\theta|\geq \theta_0>n$.
nodes.statement_short: Dispose of the case $R\equiv|\Sigma|\equiv0$; otherwise the constraint gives $|\theta|\ge\theta_0>n$.

nodes.name: Negative expansion
nodes.statement: If $\theta\leq-\theta_0<-n$, we obtain geodesic incompleteness by Proposition \ref{sing-thm}.
nodes.statement_short: Negative expansion: incompleteness by the singularity theorem.

nodes.name: Positive expansion
nodes.statement: If $\theta\geq\theta_0>n$, we have the differential inequality \eq{ \partial_t \theta\leq n-\frac{1}{n}\theta^2} so that we have the upper bound \eq{\theta \leq n\cdot\frac{e^{2t}-A_0}{e^{2t}+A_0}= \frac{n}{1-|A_0|e^{-2t}}(1+|A_0|e^{-2t})\leq n+n|A_0|e^{-2t}} where $A_0=\frac{n-\theta_0}{n+\theta_0}$. Again by the constraint equation, \eq{0\leq-R(g)+|\Sigma|^2= \frac{n-1}{n}(\theta^2-n^2)\leq Ce^{-2t}. } In particular, since $R(g)=n_1\lambda_1e^{-2x}+n_2\lambda_2 e^{-2y}$, both factors $x,y$ grow linearly, in particular, they do not converge to $-\infty$. Thus, they are geodesically complete.
nodes.statement_short: Positive expansion: completeness.

nodes.name: Riccati bound on theta
nodes.statement: If $\theta\geq\theta_0>n$, we have the differential inequality \eq{ \partial_t \theta\leq n-\frac{1}{n}\theta^2} so that we have the upper bound \eq{\theta \leq n\cdot\frac{e^{2t}-A_0}{e^{2t}+A_0}= \frac{n}{1-|A_0|e^{-2t}}(1+|A_0|e^{-2t})\leq n+n|A_0|e^{-2t}} where $A_0=\frac{n-\theta_0}{n+\theta_0}$.
nodes.statement_short: $\partial_t\theta\le n-\theta^2/n$ gives $\theta\le n+Ce^{-2t}$.

nodes.name: Completeness
nodes.statement: Again by the constraint equation, \eq{0\leq-R(g)+|\Sigma|^2= \frac{n-1}{n}(\theta^2-n^2)\leq Ce^{-2t}. } In particular, since $R(g)=n_1\lambda_1e^{-2x}+n_2\lambda_2 e^{-2y}$, both factors $x,y$ grow linearly, in particular, they do not converge to $-\infty$. Thus, they are geodesically complete.
nodes.statement_short: Constraint gives exponential decay of $-R+|\Sigma|^2$, so $x,y$ grow linearly; complete.

nodes.name: Specialize equations
nodes.statement: We have the data $n_1=2$, $n_2=1$, $\lambda_1=\lambda$, $\lambda_2=0$, so the evolution equations are \eq{\alg{x''&=3-\lambda e^{-2x}-2(x')^2-x'y'\\ y''&=3-(y')^2-2x'y'}} and the constraint equation reduce to \eq{6=2\lambda e^{-2x}+2(x')^2+4x'y'.}
nodes.statement_short: Specialize evolution and constraint to $n_1=2,n_2=1,\lambda_2=0$.

nodes.name: One-parameter family
nodes.statement: We demand $y'(0)=0$ such that we obtain a one-parameter family of solutions by prescribing $\lambda$ and $x'(0)$ such that \eq{3=\lambda+(x'(0))^2} by the constraint. Recall that we generally require $x(0)=0$. For our purposes, we additionally assume $\lambda>0$ throughout.
nodes.statement_short: Restrict to $y'(0)=0$, $3=\lambda+x'(0)^2$, $\lambda>0$.

nodes.name: Decoupled x-equation
nodes.statement: By using the constraint, the equation on $x$ decouples as \eq{\alg{x''&=3-\lambda e^{-2x}-2(x')^2-x'y'=\frac{1}{2}(3-\lambda e^{-2x}-3(x')^2).}}
nodes.statement_short: Use the constraint to decouple the $x$-equation.

nodes.name: Future incompleteness
nodes.statement: Now we show that the MGHD is future incomplete, if $\lambda<3$ and $x'(0)<0$. At first, \eq{x''(0)=3-\lambda-2x'(0)^2=(3-\lambda-(x'(0))^2)-x'(0)^2<0,} which shows that both $x$ and $x'$ are monotonically decreasing for small time. In addition, as long as $x$ and $x'$ are monotonically decreasing, we have \eq{x''=\frac{1}{2}(3-\lambda e^{-2x}-3(x')^2)\leq\frac{1}{2}(3-\lambda-2(x'(0)))\leq \frac{1}{2}x''(0)<0,} which shows that this monotonicity property holds for all time and $x$ and $x'$ are unbounded. In particular, for large time, we get \eq{x''\leq -\frac{3}{2}(x')^2. } This shows that $x'\to -\infty$ as $t$ approaches some $t_+$, since the comparison ODE is solved by $z(t)=\frac{2}{c+3t}$. By integrating, one obtains the estimate \eq{x(t)\leq C_1+\log(C_2-\frac{3}{2}t)} for some constants $C_1,C_2>0$ which shows that also $x\to-\infty$ as $t\to t_+$.
nodes.statement_short: For $\lambda<3$, $x'(0)<0$ the MGHD is future incomplete.

nodes.name: Initial decrease
nodes.statement: At first, \eq{x''(0)=3-\lambda-2x'(0)^2=(3-\lambda-(x'(0))^2)-x'(0)^2<0,} which shows that both $x$ and $x'$ are monotonically decreasing for small time.

nodes.name: Monotonicity for all time
nodes.statement: In addition, as long as $x$ and $x'$ are monotonically decreasing, we have \eq{x''=\frac{1}{2}(3-\lambda e^{-2x}-3(x')^2)\leq\frac{1}{2}(3-\lambda-2(x'(0)))\leq \frac{1}{2}x''(0)<0,} which shows that this monotonicity property holds for all time and $x$ and $x'$ are unbounded.
nodes.statement_short: Monotonicity persists; $x,x'$ unbounded.

nodes.name: Blow-up of x'
nodes.statement: In particular, for large time, we get \eq{x''\leq -\frac{3}{2}(x')^2. } This shows that $x'\to -\infty$ as $t$ approaches some $t_+$, since the comparison ODE is solved by $z(t)=\frac{2}{c+3t}$.
nodes.statement_short: $x''\le-\frac32(x')^2$ gives $x'\to-\infty$ in finite time.

nodes.name: x diverges
nodes.statement: By integrating, one obtains the estimate \eq{x(t)\leq C_1+\log(C_2-\frac{3}{2}t)} for some constants $C_1,C_2>0$ which shows that also $x\to-\infty$ as $t\to t_+$.
nodes.statement_short: Integrate to get $x\to-\infty$.
